question: Design a Content Delivery Network (CDN) Edge Architecture

sampleAnswer.strongAnswer: A Content Delivery Network (CDN) caches content at geographically distributed Edge Points of Presence (PoPs) to minimize latency to end users. Architecture: 1) Routing: uses BGP Anycast routing: all PoP servers announce the exact same IP address to the global Internet routing table. User DNS queries and TCP connections are automatically routed by Internet service providers to the topologically nearest PoP. 2) PoP Architecture: each PoP contains a Layer 4 Load Balancer (Maglev/Katran), reverse proxy cache servers (Nginx/Envoy), and SSD storage. 3) Caching Hierarchy: Edge PoPs check local memory/SSD; on a miss, they query a Regional Origin Shield PoP before falling back to the customer's Origin Server, protecting the origin from cache stampedes. 4) Purge & Invalidation: global cache invalidation messages are propagated via Pub/Sub to all edge servers within 150 milliseconds. 5) Security: DDoS protection (Anycast scrubbing) and TLS termination at the edge.

question: Design an API Gateway Service

sampleAnswer.strongAnswer: An API Gateway serves as the single secure entry point into a cloud microservices infrastructure. Architecture: 1) High-Performance Core: built on an asynchronous, non-blocking reverse proxy runtime (Envoy Proxy, Kong, or Go/Netty). 2) Dynamic Configuration: routes and upstream service endpoints are discovered dynamically using a Control Plane (e.g. Kubernetes Service Discovery or Consul) without restarting gateways. 3) Middleware Pipeline: incoming HTTP requests pass through an extensible filter chain: SSL Termination -> Rate Limiting (Redis token bucket) -> Authentication (JWT signature validation via cached JWKS public keys) -> Request Transformation & Header Enrichment (injecting `X-User-Id` and distributed tracing `Traceparent` headers) -> Upstream Routing. 4) Circuit Breaking: automatically trips open when an upstream microservice exhibits >50% errors, returning cached fallbacks or 503s immediately to prevent cascade failures.

question: Design a Distributed Logging and Distributed Tracing System (ELK / Jaeger)

sampleAnswer.strongAnswer: In microservices, a single user request can touch 20 services, requiring distributed logging and distributed tracing to troubleshoot latency and errors. Architecture: 1) Context Propagation: based on the W3C Trace Context standard, when a request enters the API Gateway, a unique `TraceId` and `SpanId` are generated and propagated across all HTTP/gRPC headers. Every downstream service logs these IDs. 2) Log Collection: lightweight agents (Fluentbit / Vector) run as daemonsets on every node, tailing container log files and shipping them asynchronously to a Kafka buffer. 3) Log Storage & Indexing: Logstash consumers pull from Kafka and index logs into Elasticsearch / OpenSearch with time-partitioned indices (e.g. `logs-2026-10-04`). 4) Trace Ingestion: OpenTelemetry collectors receive distributed spans and write trace trees to a wide-column store (Cassandra or ClickHouse). 5) UI & Visualization: Kibana for full-text log search; Jaeger for visualizing span waterfall latency graphs.

question: Design a Ticketmaster / Event Ticketing System

sampleAnswer.strongAnswer: Event ticketing requires managing massive concurrent traffic spikes for popular stadium concerts while guaranteeing that no seat is double-booked. Architecture: 1) Virtual Waiting Room: a high-throughput edge queue (Cloudflare Waiting Room or AWS SQS) throttles user entry to match database processing capacity. 2) Seat Map Caching: venue layouts and seat statuses (Available, Held, Sold) are cached in Redis and served via CDN. 3) Temporary Reservation Lock: when a user clicks 'Reserve Seat', the system acquires a distributed temporary reservation lock in Redis for 10 minutes (`SET seat:{id}:lock {userId} EX 600 NX`). The seat status flips to 'Held'. 4) Relational Transaction: once the user submits payment, a PostgreSQL transaction validates the reservation, marks the seat 'Sold', generates an encrypted QR code ticket, and commits. 5) Timeout Release: if payment fails or 10 minutes expire without checkout, a Redis TTL expiration event publishes to a topic and releases the seat back to 'Available'.
